decks.title: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Part 1: Magnetic force and the fields of currents
goals: Use the Lorentz force and describe the motion of a charge in a uniform magnetic field and in crossed fields
State the Biot–Savart law and derive the field on the axis of a circular loop
Apply Ampere’s circuital law to a long straight wire and describe the field of a solenoid

slides.heading: Moving Charges and Magnetism
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a magnetic field pushes on moving charges, and how moving charges (currents) create magnetic fields.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: Lorentz force, motion in a magnetic field, Biot–Savart law, field on a loop axis, Ampere’s law

slides.narration: In 1820 a compass needle twitched beside a current-carrying wire, and electricity and magnetism were found to be linked. In this part we see how a magnetic field pushes on a moving charge, which is how particle detectors and mass spectrometers bend beams. Then we turn it round and find the fields that currents make, using the Biot Savart law and Ampere’s law.

slides.heading: The Lorentz force
slides.body_md:
A charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec v$ in fields $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ feels
$$\vec F = q\left[\vec E + \vec v \times \vec B\right]$$
The magnetic part has size $F = qvB\sin\theta$ and is **perpendicular to both** $\vec v$ and $\vec B$. Unit of $B$: **tesla**, $1\ \text{T} = 1\ \text{N s C}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-1}$.
bullets: No magnetic force on a charge at rest, or moving parallel to $\vec B$.
The magnetic force does **no work**: it changes the direction of motion, not the speed.
For a negative charge the force is opposite to $\vec v \times \vec B$.

rows: v at angle θ to B

visual.alt: Table of the magnetic force for a charge at rest, moving parallel, perpendicular and at an angle to the field

slides.narration: The Lorentz force combines two parts. The electric part, q E, acts whether or not the charge moves. The magnetic part, q v cross B, needs motion: its size is q v B sine theta and its direction is at right angles to both the velocity and the field. Because it is always at right angles to the velocity, the magnetic force never changes a particle’s speed, only its direction.

slides.heading: Circular motion in a uniform field
slides.body_md:
If $\vec v \perp \vec B$, the force $qvB$ is always towards a fixed centre, so the charge moves in a **circle**:
$$qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{mv}{qB},\qquad T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB},\qquad f = \dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}$$
The period does not depend on the speed. With a velocity component along $\vec B$ the path is a **helix**.

slides.narration: When a charge moves at right angles to a uniform field, the magnetic force is always perpendicular to its velocity and of constant size, so it supplies a centripetal force. The charge goes round a circle of radius m v over q B. Faster particles move on bigger circles, but they take exactly the same time per revolution: the period is two pi m over q B. A velocity component along the field stretches the circle into a helix.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a proton in a magnetic field
slides.body_md: A proton moves at $2.0 \times 10^{6}$ m s$^{-1}$ perpendicular to a uniform field of $0.50$ T. Find the radius of its path and its period. ($m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg)
bullets: Step 1 — $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times 2.0 \times 10^{6}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.50} = 0.0418$ m (about 4.2 cm).
Step 2 — $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.50} \approx 1.31 \times 10^{-7}$ s.
Check — doubling the speed doubles $r$ but leaves $T$ unchanged.

slides.narration: Use r equals m v over q B with SI values: the proton circles with a radius of about four centimetres. The period, two pi m over q B, is about one point three times ten to the minus seven seconds. Notice the speed cancels from the period. That is a strong check on your algebra, and it is the reason particle accelerators can keep charges in step with a fixed-frequency supply.

slides.heading: Crossed fields: the velocity selector
slides.body_md: With $\vec E$, $\vec B$ and $\vec v$ mutually perpendicular and the forces opposite:
columns:
**Balance**
$$qE = qvB \ \Rightarrow\ v = \dfrac{E}{B}$$
Only particles with this speed pass undeflected, whatever their charge or mass.

**Faster or slower?**
- $v > E/B$: magnetic force wins, deflected one way.
- $v < E/B$: electric force wins, deflected the other way.
Used to pick one speed from a beam (J.J. Thomson’s e/m experiment, mass spectrometers).

slides.narration: Arrange an electric field and a magnetic field at right angles so that their forces on a moving charge point in opposite directions. The electric force q E is the same at all speeds, but the magnetic force q v B grows with speed. They balance only when v equals E over B, so only charges with that speed travel straight through. This velocity selector works for any charge or mass.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: selecting a speed
slides.body_md: In a velocity selector, $E = 3.0 \times 10^{4}$ V m$^{-1}$ and $B = 0.020$ T. Which speed passes undeflected? What happens to a particle twice as fast?
bullets: Step 2 — at twice this speed the magnetic force is twice the electric force, so the particle is deflected in the direction of the magnetic force.
Note — the result does not depend on the charge or mass of the particle.

slides.heading: The Biot–Savart law
slides.body_md:
A current element $I\,d\vec l$ produces at a point a distance $r$ away
$$d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,d\vec l \times \hat r}{r^2},\qquad dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}$$
with $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A$^{-1}$. $d\vec B$ is perpendicular to both $d\vec l$ and $\vec r$.
bullets: Compare with Coulomb’s law: both fall as $1/r^2$, but $d\vec B$ depends on direction through $\sin\theta$.
Zero field along the line of the element ($\theta = 0$).

slides.narration: The Biot Savart law gives the field of a tiny piece of current. Its size is mu nought over four pi, times I d l sine theta, over r squared, and its direction is at right angles to both the current element and the line to the point. Like Coulomb’s law it is an inverse square law, but it depends on the angle: a point directly in line with the element gets no field from it.

slides.heading: Field on the axis of a circular loop
slides.body_md: For a loop of radius $R$ and current $I$, every element is at distance $\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}$ from P and at $90^\circ$ to the line to P. Opposite elements’ perpendicular components cancel; the axial components add:
bullets: At the centre ($x = 0$): $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$; with $N$ turns multiply by $N$.
Direction: curl the right-hand fingers with the current; the thumb gives $\vec B$.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a flat coil
slides.body_md: A flat coil of 100 turns and radius 5.0 cm carries 2.0 A. Find the field at its centre and on its axis 5.0 cm from the centre.
bullets: Step 1 — centre: $B_0 = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 100 \times 2.0}{2 \times 0.050} = 2.51 \times 10^{-3}$ T.
Step 2 — on the axis at $x = R$: $B = \dfrac{B_0}{(1 + 1)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{B_0}{2\sqrt{2}} \approx 8.89 \times 10^{-4}$ T.
Check — about 35% of the centre value, as the graph shows.

slides.narration: At the centre, multiply mu nought by the number of turns and the current and divide by twice the radius: about two point five millitesla. At a point on the axis one radius away, R squared plus x squared is two R squared, so the field is the centre value divided by two root two, about point nine millitesla. slides.heading: Ampere’s circuital law
slides.body_md:
The line integral of $\vec B$ round any closed loop equals $\mu_0$ times the current threading the loop:
$$\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec l = \mu_0 I_\text{enc}$$
**Long straight wire:** take a circle of radius $r$; $B$ is tangential and constant on it: $B \cdot 2\pi r = \mu_0 I$, so $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.
bullets: Field lines round a wire are circles; the right-hand thumb rule gives their sense.
Like Gauss’s law, it is always true but useful only with symmetry.

Go round any closed loop adding B dot d l, and the total equals mu nought times the current passing through the loop. slides.heading: The solenoid
slides.body_md:
A long, tightly wound solenoid with $n$ turns per unit length carrying $I$ has a **uniform** field inside along its axis and nearly zero field outside:
$$B = \mu_0 n I$$
Its ends behave like the N and S poles of a bar magnet.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: wire and solenoid
slides.body_md: (a) Find the field 5.0 cm from a long straight wire carrying 10 A. (b) Find the field inside a long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carrying 2.0 A.
bullets: (a) $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 10}{0.050} = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}$ T, along circles round the wire.
(b) $B = \mu_0 nI = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1000 \times 2.0 \approx 2.51 \times 10^{-3}$ T, along the axis.
Compare — the Earth’s field is about $5 \times 10^{-5}$ T, similar to (a).

visual.alt: Field of a long straight wire falling as one over the distance from the wire

slides.narration: For the wire, mu nought over two pi is two times ten to the minus seven, so the field five centimetres away is four times ten to the minus five tesla, about the same as the Earth’s field. That is why a compass near a wire is deflected noticeably. The solenoid concentrates the field: with a thousand turns per metre and two amperes, the field inside is two and a half millitesla.

slides.body_md: Key results:

decks.title: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Part 2: Forces and torques on currents; the galvanometer
goals: Find the force on a current-carrying conductor and between two parallel currents; define the ampere
Calculate the torque on a current loop and treat it as a magnetic dipole
Explain the moving coil galvanometer and its conversion into an ammeter and a voltmeter

slides.heading: Forces and torques on currents
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the push on a wire in a magnetic field, the pull between two currents, and the turning effect that makes meters and motors work.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: force on a wire, parallel currents, the ampere, torque on a loop, galvanometer

slides.narration: A current is a stream of moving charges, so a wire carrying current in a magnetic field feels a force. In this part we find that force, see why two parallel currents attract, and use it to define the ampere. Then we find the torque on a current loop, which turns the coil of every analogue meter, and learn how a galvanometer becomes an ammeter or a voltmeter.

slides.heading: Force on a current-carrying conductor
slides.body_md:
Adding the forces $q\vec v_d \times \vec B$ on all the drifting charges in a straight conductor of length $l$:
$$\vec F = I\,\vec l \times \vec B,\qquad F = IlB\sin\theta$$
where $\vec l$ points along the current.
bullets: Largest when the wire is perpendicular to $\vec B$; zero when parallel.
Direction: perpendicular to both the wire and the field (Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the same answer).

visual.alt: Table: the force on a wire is zero parallel to the field, I l B sine theta at an angle and largest perpendicular

slides.narration: A wire carrying current contains a huge number of drifting charges, each feeling q v cross B. Add them all up and the total force on a straight piece of wire is I l cross B. Its size is I l B sine theta, largest when the wire crosses the field at right angles and zero when it lies along the field. This force drives every electric motor and loudspeaker.

slides.heading: Force between two parallel currents
slides.body_md:
Wire 1 makes a field $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$ at wire 2. The force on a length $L$ of wire 2 is $I_2 L B_1$, so the force per unit length is
$$\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$$
**Like currents attract; opposite currents repel.**

The first wire’s field at the second is mu nought I one over two pi d, and the second wire, carrying I two, feels a force I two times that field per metre. slides.heading: Defining the ampere
slides.body_md:
If two long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum carry equal currents and the force on each is $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre of length, each current is **1 ampere**:
$$\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 (1)(1)}{2\pi (1)} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$$
bullets: This is the classic definition; since 2019 the SI fixes the value of $e$ instead, but the numbers agree.
One coulomb is the charge carried by one ampere in one second.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: force between two wires
slides.body_md: Two long parallel wires 4.0 cm apart carry 5.0 A and 8.0 A in the same direction. Find the force on 1 m of either wire.

Step 2 — currents in the same direction, so the force is **attractive**.
Check — Newton’s third law: the 5 A wire feels the same force as the 8 A wire.

slides.heading: Torque on a current loop
slides.body_md:
A rectangular coil of $N$ turns, area $A$, current $I$ in a uniform field: forces on opposite sides are equal and opposite (net force zero) but form a **couple**:
$$\tau = NIAB\sin\theta,\qquad \vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B,\qquad \vec m = NI\vec A$$
$\theta$ is the angle between the normal to the coil (direction of $\vec m$) and $\vec B$.

slides.heading: The current loop as a magnetic dipole
slides.body_md: The magnetic moment $\vec m = NI\vec A$ (unit A m²) plays the role of the electric dipole moment:
columns:
**Electric dipole in $\vec E$**
- $\vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E$
- Stable when $\vec p \parallel \vec E$
- Far field $\propto p/r^3$

**Current loop in $\vec B$**
- $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$
- Stable when $\vec m \parallel \vec B$
- Far field on the axis $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3}$

slides.narration: A small current loop behaves exactly like a magnetic dipole. Its magnetic moment, N I A, points along the normal given by the right-hand rule. In a uniform field it feels a torque m cross B that turns it into line with the field, just as an electric dipole turns in an electric field. Far away, its field on the axis is mu nought over four pi times two m over r cubed, the same form as the electric dipole field.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: torque on a coil
slides.body_md: A rectangular coil of 50 turns, 4.0 cm × 5.0 cm, carries 0.50 A in a uniform field of 0.20 T. The normal to the coil makes $30^\circ$ with the field. Find the magnetic moment and the torque, and the largest possible torque.
bullets: Step 2 — $\tau = mB\sin 30^\circ = 0.050 \times 0.20 \times 0.5 = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ N m.
Step 3 — largest at $90^\circ$: $\tau_\text{max} = mB = 0.010$ N m.

visual.alt: Worked table: magnetic moment 0.050 ampere square metre, torque 5.0 times ten to the minus three newton metre at 30 degrees and 1.0 times ten to the minus two at most

slides.narration: First find the area in square metres, two times ten to the minus three. The magnetic moment is turns times current times area, zero point zero five ampere square metre. Multiply by B and by sine thirty degrees to get five times ten to the minus three newton metre. When the normal is at right angles to the field the torque doubles to its maximum, one times ten to the minus two newton metre.

slides.heading: The moving coil galvanometer
slides.body_md:
A coil on a soft-iron core sits in a **radial** field between concave pole pieces, so $\vec B$ is always in the plane of the coil and the torque is $NIAB$ at every angle. A spring provides a restoring torque $k\phi$. At equilibrium:
$$NIAB = k\phi \Rightarrow \phi = \left(\dfrac{NAB}{k}\right) I$$
bullets: The deflection is proportional to the current: a linear scale.
**Current sensitivity** $\phi/I = NAB/k$; **voltage sensitivity** $\phi/V = NAB/(kG)$.
Increasing $N$ raises current sensitivity, but also the resistance $G$, so voltage sensitivity need not rise.

visual.alt: Table of galvanometer parts and their purposes: pole pieces, soft-iron core, spring, pointer and scale

slides.narration: In a moving coil galvanometer the magnet’s pole pieces are curved and a soft-iron cylinder sits inside the coil, so the field is radial. Then the plane of the coil always lies along the field, and the torque is N I A B whatever the angle. A spring twists back with a torque proportional to the deflection. Balancing the two, the deflection is proportional to the current, giving an evenly spaced scale.

slides.heading: Galvanometer to ammeter and voltmeter
slides.body_md: A galvanometer (resistance $G$, full-scale current $I_g$) can be converted:
bullets: **Ammeter (range $I$):** small **shunt** $S$ in parallel, $S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g}$. Total resistance is very small.
**Voltmeter (range $V$):** large **series** resistance $R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G$. Total resistance is very large.

To measure large currents, connect a small shunt resistance in parallel so that most of the current bypasses the coil; the ammeter then has very small resistance and hardly disturbs the circuit it is put in series with. To measure voltage, add a large resistance in series, so the meter draws very little current from the points it is connected across.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: converting a galvanometer
slides.body_md: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 2.0 mA. Find (a) the shunt needed to make a 0–1.0 A ammeter, (b) the series resistance needed for a 0–10 V voltmeter.
bullets: (a) $S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g} = \dfrac{0.0020 \times 50}{1.0 - 0.0020} \approx 0.100$ Ω, in parallel.
(b) $R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G = \dfrac{10}{0.0020} - 50 = 4950$ Ω, in series.
Check — the ammeter’s total resistance is below 0.1 Ω; the voltmeter’s is 5000 Ω.

sections.heading: 1. Lorentz force and motion of charges
sections.body_md:
**Lorentz force:** $\vec F = q(\vec E + \vec v \times \vec B)$. Magnetic part $qvB\sin\theta$, perpendicular to $\vec v$ and $\vec B$; zero for $v = 0$ or $\vec v \parallel \vec B$; does **no work** (speed constant). Unit of $B$: tesla (T).

**Uniform $\vec B$, $\vec v \perp \vec B$:** circle with $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$, period $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$, frequency $f = \dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}$ — independent of speed. With a component of $\vec v$ along $\vec B$: a **helix** (pitch $= v_\parallel T$).

**Crossed fields (velocity selector):** $\vec E \perp \vec B \perp \vec v$ with opposing forces; undeflected when $qE = qvB$, i.e. $v = E/B$, for any charge or mass.

key_terms.definition_md: The total force on a charge in electric and magnetic fields, $q(\vec E + \vec v \times \vec B)$.
Field in which a charge of 1 C moving at 1 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to it feels 1 N.

sections.heading: 2. Biot–Savart law and the circular loop
sections.body_md:
**Biot–Savart law:** $d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec l \times \hat r}{r^2}$, $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}$, $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A$^{-1}$.

**Axis of a circular loop** (radius $R$, distance $x$): each element is at distance $\sqrt{R^2+x^2}$ and perpendicular to the line to P, so $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{R^2+x^2}$. Perpendicular components cancel in pairs; axial components $dB\cos\alpha$ with $\cos\alpha = R/\sqrt{R^2+x^2}$ add over $\oint dl = 2\pi R$:
$$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$$
At the centre $B = \mu_0 I/2R$ ($N$ turns: multiply by $N$). Far away ($x \gg R$): $B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^3}$ with $m = I\pi R^2$. Direction: right-hand rule (fingers with the current, thumb along $\vec B$).

sections.heading: 3. Ampere’s circuital law
sections.body_md:
$$\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec l = \mu_0 I_\text{enc}$$
- **Long straight wire:** circle of radius $r$ round the wire; $B$ tangential and constant: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$. Field lines are concentric circles (right-hand thumb rule).
- **Long solenoid** ($n$ turns per metre): uniform field inside along the axis, $B = \mu_0 nI$; nearly zero outside; behaves like a bar magnet (treated qualitatively in the syllabus).

Like Gauss’s law, Ampere’s law always holds but gives $B$ easily only when symmetry makes $B$ constant along the chosen loop.

sections.heading: 4. Forces on currents; the ampere
sections.body_md:
**Force on a straight conductor:** $\vec F = I\vec l \times \vec B$, $F = IlB\sin\theta$.

**Two long parallel wires** a distance $d$ apart: $\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$. Currents in the **same** direction **attract**; opposite currents **repel**. The forces on the two wires are equal and opposite.

**Ampere (classic definition):** the current which, in each of two long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre of length.

key_terms.definition_md: Current in two long parallel wires 1 m apart giving a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre between them.

sections.heading: 5. Torque on a current loop; magnetic dipole
sections.body_md:
A coil of $N$ turns, area $A$, current $I$ in a uniform field: net force zero; torque
$$\tau = NIAB\sin\theta,\qquad \vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B,\qquad \vec m = NI\vec A$$
($\theta$ between the normal to the coil and $\vec B$). Maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to $\vec B$; zero when it is perpendicular. Stable equilibrium with $\vec m$ along $\vec B$.

A current loop is a **magnetic dipole** (moment in A m²), the analogue of an electric dipole: $\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E$ ↔ $\vec\tau = \vec m\times\vec B$; far field $\propto m/r^3$.

key_terms.definition_md: $\vec m = NI\vec A$, directed along the normal given by the right-hand rule.

sections.heading: 6. Moving coil galvanometer
sections.body_md:
Coil on a soft-iron core in a **radial** field (concave pole pieces), so the torque is $NIAB$ at all deflections; spring restoring torque $k\phi$. Equilibrium: $\phi = \dfrac{NAB}{k}I$ — linear scale.

- **Current sensitivity** $\phi/I = NAB/k$; **voltage sensitivity** $\phi/V = NAB/kG$.
- Raising $N$ raises current sensitivity but also $G$, so voltage sensitivity may not rise.

**Conversions** ($G$, full-scale $I_g$):
- Ammeter of range $I$: shunt $S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g}$ in **parallel** (very low total resistance; connected in series).
- Voltmeter of range $V$: $R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G$ in **series** (very high total resistance; connected in parallel).

key_terms.definition_md: Field whose lines point along radii, so the plane of the coil always lies along the field.
Small resistance connected in parallel with a galvanometer.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A steady magnetic field cannot change the kinetic energy of a charged particle moving through it.
questions.solution_md: True. The magnetic force $q\vec v \times \vec B$ is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work; only the direction of motion changes.

questions.stem_md: An electron moves towards the right across the page through a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. The magnetic force on it is

options.text_md: towards the top of the page
towards the bottom of the page

questions.solution_md: For a positive charge, $\vec v \times \vec B$ (right × into) points to the top of the page; the electron is negative, so the force points to the bottom — option (b).

questions.stem_md: An electron moves at 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a uniform field of 1.0 × 10⁻³ T. Find the radius of its path, in centimetres. (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)

A proton and an alpha particle (charge $2e$, mass about $4m_p$) enter the same uniform magnetic field with the same speed, perpendicular to the field. The ratio of the radius of the alpha particle’s path to that of the proton is
questions.solution_md: $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$: $\dfrac{r_\alpha}{r_p} = \dfrac{4m/2e}{m/e} = 2$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A proton and a deuteron (same charge, twice the mass) have the SAME kinetic energy and move perpendicular to the same uniform magnetic field. The ratio $r_d / r_p$ of the radii of their paths is
questions.solution_md: $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$, so with the same $K$ and $q$, $r \propto \sqrt{m}$: the ratio is $\sqrt{2}$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The speed of a charged particle moving in a circle in a uniform magnetic field is doubled. Its period of revolution
questions.solution_md: $T = 2\pi m/qB$ does not involve $v$: the radius doubles, and so does the distance per turn — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A proton enters a uniform magnetic field with its velocity at $30^\circ$ to the field. Its path is

options.text_md: a circle in a plane perpendicular to the field
a straight line along the field
a helix with its axis along the field

questions.solution_md: The component of $\vec v$ along $\vec B$ is unchanged, while the perpendicular component makes the proton circle: together they give a helix — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a velocity selector the magnetic field is 0.050 T. What electric field (in V m⁻¹) lets ions moving at 4.0 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ pass undeflected?
A proton moves at 5.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at 30° to a uniform field of 0.40 T. Find the magnetic force on it, in piconewtons (1 pN = 10⁻¹² N).
questions.solution_md: $F = qvB\sin 30^\circ = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 5.0 \times 10^{6} \times 0.40 \times 0.5 = 1.6 \times 10^{-13}$ N. In pN: $1.6 \times 10^{-13} \times 10^{12} = 0.16$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A charged particle moving through a magnetic field always experiences a magnetic force.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic force on a moving charge is $q\vec v \times \vec B$.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: if $\vec v$ is parallel or antiparallel to $\vec B$, $\vec v \times \vec B = 0$ and there is no force — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of magnetic field is the ___.
questions.solution_md: The **tesla** (T); 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a charged particle entering a uniform magnetic field at an angle (neither along nor perpendicular to it) moves in a helix.

answer.model_answer_md: Split $\vec v$ into components **along** $\vec B$ and **perpendicular** to it. The parallel component feels **no force**, so it stays constant and carries the particle along the field. The perpendicular component feels a force $qv_\perp B$ at right angles to it, so it produces **circular motion**. Circling while drifting steadily along the field gives a helix.

questions.solution_md: Resolve v along and perpendicular to B.

marking_scheme.step: Perpendicular component gives circular motion: helix

questions.stem_md: A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ moves with speed $v$ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$. Show that its path is a circle, find its radius, and show that its period does not depend on its speed.

answer.model_answer_md: The force $qvB$ is always perpendicular to $\vec v$, so the speed stays constant and the force has constant size: it acts as a **centripetal force**, so the path is a circle. $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ gives $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$. Period $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$, which contains no $v$: a faster particle moves on a proportionally larger circle in the same time.

questions.solution_md: Equate qvB to mv²/r; then T = 2πr/v.

marking_scheme.step: Force perpendicular to v, constant speed: circle

questions.stem_md: The current in a circular loop is kept the same but the radius of the loop is doubled. The field at its centre becomes
questions.solution_md: $B = \mu_0 I/2R$ is inversely proportional to $R$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A circular coil of 50 turns and radius 10 cm carries 1.5 A. Find the field at its centre, in millitesla (mT).
questions.solution_md: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 50 \times 1.5}{2 \times 0.10} \approx 4.71 \times 10^{-4}$ T. In mT: $4.71 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{3} = 0.471$.

questions.stem_md: The field at the centre of a circular loop is $B_0$. At a point on its axis at a distance $\sqrt{3}R$ from the centre, the field is
A wire bent into a semicircle of radius $R$ carries current $I$ (the straight leads point radially and contribute nothing). The field at the centre of the semicircle is
questions.solution_md: Every element is at distance $R$ and perpendicular to the radius, so the Biot–Savart contributions add: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I(\pi R)}{R^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4R}$, half the full-loop value — option (c).

questions.stem_md: According to the Biot–Savart law, the field produced by a short current element at a point lying on the line of the element (ahead of it) is
questions.solution_md: For a point on the line of the element, $\theta = 0$ and $\sin\theta = 0$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A circular loop lies flat on a table and, seen from above, carries current anticlockwise. State the direction of the field at its centre and explain how you found it.

answer.model_answer_md: The field at the centre points **vertically upwards** (out of the table, towards the viewer). Curl the fingers of the **right hand** in the direction of the current (anticlockwise seen from above); the thumb points up, giving the field direction at the centre.

questions.solution_md: Right-hand rule for a loop.

questions.stem_md: Match each current arrangement in Column A with its magnetic field in Column B.

options.text_md: Centre of a circular loop of radius R
Inside a long solenoid, n turns per metre
Centre of a semicircular arc of radius R

questions.solution_md: Wire → μ₀I/2πr (1 → r); loop centre → μ₀I/2R (2 → p); solenoid → μ₀nI (3 → s); semicircle → μ₀I/4R (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: Find the magnetic field 4.0 cm from a long straight wire carrying 6.0 A, in microtesla (μT).
A closed loop encloses two long wires: one carries 3 A into the page and the other 5 A out of the page. The magnitude of $\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec l$ round the loop is
questions.solution_md: Only the net enclosed current counts: $5 - 3 = 2$ A, so the integral is $\mu_0 \times 2$ in magnitude — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A solenoid 50 cm long has 500 turns and carries 2.0 A. Find the field inside it, near the middle, in millitesla.
A long solenoid is rewound with twice as many turns over the same length, and the current is halved. The field inside
questions.solution_md: $B = \mu_0 nI$: $n$ doubles and $I$ halves, so $nI$ is unchanged — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Two long parallel wires carry equal currents in the SAME direction. The magnetic field at the point midway between them is

options.text_md: twice the field of one wire
equal to the field of one wire
along the line joining the wires

questions.solution_md: At the midpoint the two fields are equal in size and, by the right-hand rule, opposite in direction — option (c). (Opposite currents would give twice one wire’s field.)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ampere’s circuital law gives the field of a long straight wire very simply.

**Reason (R):** By symmetry, the field is tangential and has the same size at every point of a circle centred on the wire.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and the symmetry in R is exactly why $\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec l$ reduces to $B \cdot 2\pi r$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A long straight wire carrying 15 A runs north–south, 5.0 cm above a compass. The horizontal component of the Earth’s field there is 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T. Find the wire’s field at the compass and say whether the compass will deflect noticeably.

answer.model_answer_md: $B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 15}{0.050} = 6.0 \times 10^{-5}$ T, at right angles to the wire (east–west), about $1.5$ times the Earth’s horizontal field. The compass points along the resultant, so it deflects **a lot** (about $56^\circ$, since $\tan\theta = 6.0/4.0$).

questions.solution_md: Compare the wire’s field with the Earth’s horizontal field.

marking_scheme.step: Comparable with/larger than Earth’s field: large deflection

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two long parallel wires carrying currents in opposite directions repel each other.

**Reason (R):** Each wire lies in the magnetic field of the other, and the force $I\vec l \times \vec B$ on it points away from the other wire.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; working out $\vec B$ of one wire at the other and then $I\vec l \times \vec B$ gives a force directed away, which explains the repulsion — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A straight wire 0.50 m long carries 4.0 A at right angles to a uniform field of 0.30 T. Find the force on it, in newtons.
questions.solution_md: $F = IlB = 4.0 \times 0.50 \times 0.30 = 0.6$ N.

questions.stem_md: A closed loop of wire of any shape carries a current and lies in a UNIFORM magnetic field. The net magnetic force on the loop is

options.text_md: $IlB$, where $l$ is the length of wire
largest when the loop is circular

questions.solution_md: $\vec F = I\left(\oint d\vec l\right) \times \vec B$, and $\oint d\vec l = 0$ for a closed loop — option (b). (There can still be a torque.)

questions.stem_md: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 20 A and 30 A. Find the force per metre of length between them, in millinewtons per metre (mN m⁻¹).
A light, loosely wound metal spring hangs vertically with its lower end just dipping into mercury. When a current is passed through the spring, it

options.text_md: stays still, because the forces cancel
contracts, because neighbouring turns carry parallel currents and attract

questions.solution_md: Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract and the spring shortens — option (d). (It then lifts out of the mercury, the circuit breaks, and the spring falls back: it oscillates.)

questions.stem_md: Three long parallel wires lie in one plane, equally spaced, each carrying the same current in the same direction. The net force on the middle wire is

options.text_md: twice the force between two neighbours

questions.solution_md: The middle wire is attracted equally by the wires on either side, so the forces cancel — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Define one ampere using the force between two parallel currents.

answer.model_answer_md: One ampere is the steady current which, flowing in each of two **infinitely long**, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed **1 m apart in vacuum**, produces between them a force of **$2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre** of length.

questions.solution_md: State the arrangement and the force per metre.

marking_scheme.step: Two long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum

questions.stem_md: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 10 A each in OPPOSITE directions. Find (a) the field midway between them, (b) the force per metre on each wire, and state whether they attract or repel.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Each wire gives $\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 10}{0.050} = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}$ T at the midpoint; for opposite currents the two fields point the **same** way there, so $B = 8.0 \times 10^{-5}$ T.
(b) $\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 10 \times 10}{0.10} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ N m$^{-1}$; opposite currents **repel**.

questions.solution_md: Add the two wire fields at the midpoint; then μ₀I₁I₂/2πd.

questions.stem_md: A current-carrying coil is free to rotate in a uniform magnetic field. The torque on it is zero when

options.text_md: the plane of the coil is parallel to the field
the plane of the coil is at 45° to the field
the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field

questions.solution_md: Then the normal (and $\vec m$) is along $\vec B$, so $\theta = 0$ and $\tau = NIAB\sin\theta = 0$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A circular coil of 100 turns and radius 2.0 cm carries 0.50 A. Find its magnetic moment, in A m² (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $m = NI\pi R^2 = 100 \times 0.50 \times \pi \times 0.020^2 \approx 0.0628$ A m².

questions.stem_md: A coil of 20 turns and area 25 cm² carries 2.0 A in a uniform field of 0.50 T, with the plane of the coil PARALLEL to the field. Find the torque on it, in N m.
questions.solution_md: Plane parallel to $\vec B$ means the normal is perpendicular: $\theta = 90^\circ$. $\tau = NIAB = 20 \times 2.0 \times 25 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.50 = 0.050$ N m (the maximum).

questions.stem_md: Equal lengths of the same wire are bent into a circle and into a square, and the same current is passed through each. Which has the larger magnetic moment?

options.text_md: It depends on the field they are placed in

questions.solution_md: $m = IA$. For perimeter $L$: circle area $L^2/4\pi \approx 0.080L^2$; square area $L^2/16 \approx 0.063L^2$. The circle encloses more area — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each quantity for an electric dipole in Column A with its analogue for a current loop (magnetic dipole) in Column B.
questions.solution_md: p ↔ m = NIA (1 → q); p × E ↔ m × B (2 → s); stable alignment (3 → p); far field ∝ 1/r³ (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: Derive an expression for the torque on a rectangular coil of $N$ turns, sides $a$ and $b$, carrying current $I$ in a uniform field $B$, when the normal to the coil makes angle $\theta$ with the field.

answer.model_answer_md: Let the sides of length $b$ be perpendicular to $\vec B$ (the rotation axis is parallel to them). On each such side the force is $NIbB$, equal and opposite on the two sides. The forces on the other two sides are equal, opposite and along the same line (they cancel without torque). The two forces $NIbB$ act along parallel lines separated by $a\sin\theta$, forming a couple: $\tau = NIbB \times a\sin\theta = NIAB\sin\theta$ with $A = ab$. In vector form $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$, $\vec m = NI\vec A$.

questions.solution_md: Find the couple formed by the forces on the two sides perpendicular to B.

marking_scheme.step: Forces NIbB on the two sides, net force zero

questions.stem_md: Which statement about an ideal ammeter is correct?

options.text_md: It has zero resistance and is connected in series
It has infinite resistance and is connected in series
It has zero resistance and is connected in parallel
It has infinite resistance and is connected in parallel

questions.solution_md: In series, a zero-resistance ammeter does not change the current it measures — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The pole pieces of a moving coil galvanometer are made concave and a soft-iron core is placed inside the coil so that

options.text_md: the field is uniform and parallel to the coil’s normal
the field is radial, making the deflection proportional to the current

questions.solution_md: In a radial field the plane of the coil is always along $\vec B$, so the torque is $NIAB$ at every deflection and $\phi \propto I$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer of resistance 100 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 1.0 mA. Find the shunt needed to make it an ammeter of range 0–0.10 A, in ohms (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g} = \dfrac{0.0010 \times 100}{0.10 - 0.0010} = \dfrac{0.1}{0.099} \approx 1.01$ Ω, in parallel.

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer of resistance 20 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 5.0 mA. Find the resistance to be connected in series to make it a voltmeter of range 0–15 V, in ohms.
A galvanometer coil is rewound with twice as many turns of the same wire (so its resistance also doubles), everything else unchanged. Its current sensitivity and voltage sensitivity become
questions.solution_md: Current sensitivity $NAB/k$ doubles with $N$. Voltage sensitivity $NAB/(kG)$: both $N$ and $G$ double, so it is unchanged — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** To increase the range of an ammeter, a larger shunt resistance must be used.

**Reason (R):** In an ammeter, the shunt carries most of the current.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: a larger range needs a **smaller** shunt, $S = I_gG/(I - I_g)$, so that more current bypasses the coil — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Why does a moving coil galvanometer use a soft-iron core inside the coil? Give two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: The soft-iron core (with concave pole pieces) makes the field **radial**, so the torque is $NIAB$ at every angle and the scale is **linear**. It also **concentrates** the field lines, increasing $B$ and so the **sensitivity** of the galvanometer.

questions.solution_md: Radial field and stronger field.

marking_scheme.step: Makes the field radial: linear scale

questions.stem_md: A student connects a voltmeter of resistance 500 Ω across a 10 kΩ resistor to measure its voltage. Evaluate this choice of meter.

answer.model_answer_md: Poor choice. The 500 Ω meter in **parallel** with 10 kΩ makes a combination of only about **476 Ω**, so it draws a large current and **changes** the voltage it is meant to measure. A voltmeter should have a resistance **much larger** than the resistor (say ≥ 1 MΩ) so that it draws negligible current.

questions.solution_md: Compare the meter resistance with the resistance it is connected across.

marking_scheme.step: Voltmeter must have very high resistance

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer has resistance 60 Ω and full-scale current 2.0 mA. Show how to convert it into (a) an ammeter of range 0–3.0 A and (b) a voltmeter of range 0–6.0 V, finding the resistance needed in each case and how it is connected.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Shunt in **parallel**: $S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g} = \dfrac{0.0020 \times 60}{3.0 - 0.0020} \approx 0.0400$ Ω (about 0.04 Ω).
(b) Resistance in **series**: $R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G = \dfrac{6.0}{0.0020} - 60 = 2940$ Ω.
The ammeter then has a very small total resistance; the voltmeter a large one (3000 Ω).

questions.solution_md: Shunt for the ammeter, series resistance for the voltmeter.

questions.stem_md: (a) State the Biot–Savart law in vector form. (b) Use it to derive the magnetic field at a point on the axis of a circular loop of radius $R$ carrying current $I$, at a distance $x$ from its centre. (c) Find the field at the centre of a single loop of radius 10 cm carrying 5.0 A.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec l \times \hat r}{r^2}$, where $\hat r$ points from the element to the point.

(b) Every element $d\vec l$ of the loop is at distance $r = \sqrt{R^2 + x^2}$ from P and perpendicular to $\vec r$, so $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{R^2 + x^2}$, directed perpendicular to $\vec r$. Resolve it into a component along the axis, $dB\cos\alpha$, and one perpendicular to it. For diametrically opposite elements the perpendicular components cancel. With $\cos\alpha = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}}$:
$$B = \oint \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{R^2 + x^2}\cdot\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R}{4\pi (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}\cdot 2\pi R = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$$
along the axis (right-hand rule).

(c) At the centre $x = 0$: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 5.0}{2 \times 0.10} \approx 3.14 \times 10^{-5}$ T.

questions.solution_md: Equal-size contributions from every element; perpendicular parts cancel; integrate dl round the loop.

marking_scheme.step: dB for an element and its direction

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive an expression for the force per unit length between two long straight parallel wires carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$, a distance $d$ apart. (b) Show that like currents attract. (c) Use the result to define the ampere. (d) Find the force on 2.0 m of either wire when $I_1 = 4.0$ A, $I_2 = 6.0$ A and $d = 3.0$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) By Ampere’s law, wire 1 produces at wire 2 a field $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$, perpendicular to wire 2. The force on a length $L$ of wire 2 is $F = I_2 L B_1$, so $\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$. By symmetry wire 1 feels an equal and opposite force.

(b) Let both currents point up the page with wire 2 to the right of wire 1. The right-hand rule gives $\vec B_1$ at wire 2 into the page. $I_2\vec L \times \vec B_1$ (up × into) points to the left, towards wire 1: **attraction**.

(c) **One ampere** is the current in each of two long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum that gives a force of $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre.

(d) $\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 4.0 \times 6.0}{0.030} = 1.6 \times 10^{-4}$ N m$^{-1}$, so on 2.0 m: $F = 3.2 \times 10^{-4}$ N (attractive if the currents are in the same direction).

questions.solution_md: Field of one wire at the other, then F = ILB.

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain the principle and working of a moving coil galvanometer, including the role of the radial field. (b) Define current sensitivity and show that it equals $NAB/k$. (c) A galvanometer coil has 30 turns of area 1.5 × 10⁻³ m² in a radial field of 0.20 T, and the spring constant is 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ N m rad⁻¹. Find the deflection for a current of 1.0 μA.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Principle:** a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field feels a torque. The coil, wound on a soft-iron core, hangs between concave pole pieces, so the field is **radial**: the plane of the coil is always along $\vec B$ and the deflecting torque is $NIAB$ at every angle. A spring provides a restoring torque $k\phi$. The coil turns until $NIAB = k\phi$, so $\phi = \dfrac{NAB}{k}I$: the deflection is proportional to the current and the scale is linear.

(b) **Current sensitivity** is the deflection per unit current, $\dfrac{\phi}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{k}$, from the equilibrium condition.

(c) $\dfrac{\phi}{I} = \dfrac{30 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.20}{3.0 \times 10^{-8}} = 3.0 \times 10^{5}$ rad A$^{-1}$, so for 1.0 μA: $\phi = 0.30$ rad (about 17°).

questions.solution_md: Balance NIAB with kφ.

marking_scheme.step: Radial field: torque NIAB at all angles

questions.stem_md: (a) Write the Lorentz force on a charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec v$ in fields $\vec E$ and $\vec B$, and show that a magnetic field does no work on the charge. (b) Electrons pass undeflected through crossed fields $E = 1.0 \times 10^{4}$ V m$^{-1}$ and $B = 0.025$ T. Find their speed. (c) They then enter a region with only a magnetic field of 0.10 T, perpendicular to their velocity. Find the radius of their path. (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\vec F = q(\vec E + \vec v \times \vec B)$. The magnetic part is perpendicular to $\vec v$, so its power $\vec F\cdot\vec v = q(\vec v \times \vec B)\cdot\vec v = 0$: it does no work and the speed does not change.

(b) Undeflected: $qE = qvB$, so $v = \dfrac{E}{B} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{4}}{0.025} = 4.0 \times 10^{5}$ m s$^{-1}$.

(c) $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 4.0 \times 10^{5}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.10} = 2.27 \times 10^{-5}$ m (about 23 μm).

questions.solution_md: F·v = 0 for the magnetic part; v = E/B; r = mv/qB.

questions.stem_md: (a) Show that a current loop in a uniform field experiences no net force but a torque $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$. (b) A rectangular coil of 40 turns, 6.0 cm × 4.0 cm, carries 0.80 A in a field of 0.50 T. Find its magnetic moment and the torque when its normal makes $60^\circ$ with the field. (c) In which orientation is the coil in stable equilibrium?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For a rectangular coil, the forces on opposite sides are equal and opposite: those on the sides parallel to the rotation axis ($NIbB$ each) act along parallel lines a distance $a\sin\theta$ apart, and those on the other two sides act along one line. The net force is zero, but the first pair forms a couple: $\tau = NIbB\,a\sin\theta = NIAB\sin\theta$, i.e. $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$ with $\vec m = NI\vec A$.

(b) $m = NIA = 40 \times 0.80 \times 0.060 \times 0.040 = 0.0768$ A m². $\tau = mB\sin 60^\circ = 0.0768 \times 0.50 \times 0.866 \approx 0.0333$ N m.

(c) **Stable** when $\vec m$ is along $\vec B$ (plane of the coil perpendicular to the field): the torque is zero and a small twist produces a torque that restores it.

questions.solution_md: Couple from the two sides; then m = NIA and τ = mB sin θ.

marking_scheme.step: Couple and τ = NIAB sin θ
Stable when m is along B

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic field just outside the middle of a long solenoid is very strong.

Choose the correct option.

A is true, but R is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a moving coil galvanometer the deflection is directly proportional to the current.

**Reason (R):** The radial field keeps the plane of the coil along the field at every deflection, so the deflecting torque is always NIAB.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A current-carrying loop placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences a net force.
questions.solution_md: False. The forces on opposite sides cancel, so the net force is zero; the loop experiences only a torque. (In a non-uniform field there can be a net force.)

questions.stem_md: True or false? The field inside a long, tightly wound solenoid does not depend on the radius of its turns.
questions.solution_md: True. $B = \mu_0 nI$ depends only on the turns per unit length and the current.

questions.solution_md: Tesla metre per **ampere** (T m A⁻¹), equivalent to N A⁻².

questions.stem_md: A proton moves along a helical path in a uniform magnetic field. If the field is doubled (the velocity components unchanged at that instant), the pitch of the helix
questions.solution_md: Pitch $= v_\parallel T$ and $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$: doubling $B$ halves $T$ and so halves the pitch — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two concentric circular loops lie in the same plane, with radii $R$ and $2R$. Each carries current $I$, but in opposite senses. The field at the common centre is

questions.solution_md: $m = NI\pi R^2$, so doubling $R$ multiplies $m$ by 4 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A straight wire 20 cm long carrying 3.0 A in a uniform field of 0.50 T experiences a force of 0.15 N. Find the angle between the wire and the field, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: $F = IlB\sin\theta$, so $\sin\theta = \dfrac{0.15}{3.0 \times 0.20 \times 0.50} = 0.5$, so $\theta = 30$ degrees.

questions.stem_md: A voltmeter made from a galvanometer has a total resistance of 2000 Ω and a range of 0–5 V. What extra resistance must be added in series to extend its range to 0–15 V?
questions.solution_md: Full-scale current $I_g = 5/2000 = 0.0025$ A. For 15 V the total must be $15/0.0025 = 6000$ Ω, so add $6000 - 2000 = 4000$ Ω — option (d).

They move on circles of equal radius, in opposite senses
The proton’s circle is much smaller
They move on equal circles in the same sense

answer.model_answer_md: Take $\vec v$ away from you and $\vec B$ up. For a **positive** charge, $\vec v \times \vec B$ points to your **right** (forward × up = right). The electrons are **negative**, so the force — and the deflection of the spot — is to your **left**.

questions.stem_md: Ampere’s circuital law is true for every closed loop. Why, then, is it not used to find the field of a short straight segment of wire?

answer.model_answer_md: Ampere’s law gives $B$ easily only when **symmetry** makes $B$ constant and tangential (or zero) along a loop, so that $\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec l$ becomes $B \times$ length. Near a short segment the field varies along any loop, so the integral cannot be simplified; the **Biot–Savart law** is used instead.

questions.solution_md: The law needs symmetry to be useful.
